summary: Describes how to use RSVP to request the Controlled-Load and Guaranteed quality-of-service controls from the integrated services framework. It defines how the needed parameters are carried in RSVP messages.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2210 defines how RSVP carries information for Controlled-Load and Guaranteed network service. Senders describe their traffic, network elements report path conditions, and receivers use that information to request a reservation.

subtitle: How RSVP carries service requests and path information for two integrated-services quality levels.

tldr.problem: RSVP carries reservation objects without interpreting their service-specific contents. Controlled-Load and Guaranteed services need common object formats to exchange traffic descriptions, path information and reservation requests.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SENDER_TSPEC, ADSPEC and FLOWSPEC objects. Senders send traffic details downstream, network elements update path details, and receivers send a service request upstream.
tldr.outcome: The formats allow receivers to choose between Controlled-Load and Guaranteed service using information gathered along the path. RFC 2210 is a Proposed Standard; the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 2210 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How RSVP and Integrated Services Fit Together
sections.content:
Integrated services lets an application request a controlled level of delivery for its packets. Network elements along the route provide the service, while a setup protocol carries the application's requirements and the network's information back and forth.

RSVP does not define the contents of objects used to invoke a quality-of-service control service. RFC 2210 defines the use and format of FLOWSPEC, ADSPEC and SENDER_TSPEC for Controlled-Load and Guaranteed services. It does not define RSVP accounting or policy objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications need to tell the network what traffic they will send and what delivery service they want. RFC 2210 defines the RSVP message fields that carry those details for two services.

sections.title: Three Objects Carry Different Information
sections.content:
SENDER_TSPEC describes traffic produced by a sender. It travels toward receivers and is not changed by intermediate network elements. The shared traffic specification works with either service defined here.

ADSPEC carries information from senders and network elements toward receivers, including service availability and path properties. Each RSVP-aware hop updates and summarizes this information. FLOWSPEC carries a receiver's service choice and reservation parameters upstream; reservation merging can change it along the route.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender reports the traffic it expects to produce. Each network hop adds or updates information about the route, and the receiver sends its reservation request back toward the sender.

sections.title: From a Sender's Path Message to a Reservation
sections.content:
The sender registers with RSVP and provides a Sender TSpec, which RSVP places in a PATH message. The sender also supplies an initial ADSPEC. Network elements pass the ADSPEC to traffic control, which updates the information for services the element supports. An unsupported service is reported with a break bit.

At the receiver, the application uses the arriving TSpec and ADSPEC to choose a service and reservation parameters. RSVP carries those parameters in a FLOWSPEC in a RESV message toward the sender. Each RSVP-aware hop requests resources from the selected service, and the merged FLOWSPEC eventually reaches the senders.

In RSVP version 1, all receivers in a session must choose the same service. A sender can limit the available choice by leaving that service's fragment out of its ADSPEC.
sections.plainLanguage: Path information travels from sender to receiver and is updated along the route. The receiver then requests a service, and that request travels back through the network.

sections.title: Break Bits and the Smallest Path MTU
sections.content:
An ADSPEC break bit tells the receiver whether a part of the path could not support RSVP quality-of-service processing. A break bit in the general-parameters fragment means some hop does not support RSVP and integrated services; other ADSPEC values may then be unreliable. A service-specific break bit means a hop supports RSVP but not that service.

For packet sizing, each sender reports its largest packet size in the TSpec's M field. The ADSPEC's PATH_MTU reports the smallest supported MTU on the path. A receiver uses the smallest applicable value in its request, and merge points forward the smaller packet-size value. Packets larger than the resulting reservation MTU may receive best-effort service instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A break bit warns that a network hop cannot provide a particular service, or cannot update service information at all. The path MTU tells the receiver the largest packet size the reservation can cover across the route.

sections.title: Reservation and Path Object Contents
sections.content:
The SENDER_TSPEC contains a Token_Bucket_TSpec, service number 1 and parameter number 127. Its fields describe token rate r, bucket size b, peak rate p, minimum policed unit m and maximum packet size M. A zero value for m is illegal.

A Controlled-Load FLOWSPEC uses service number 5 and the shared TSpec. A Guaranteed FLOWSPEC uses service number 2, the TSpec and an RSpec (parameter 130) containing rate R and slack term S. The ADSPEC has a general-parameters fragment first, followed by any included service fragments in service-number order.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic fields say how fast data can arrive and how large packets can be. A Guaranteed request adds its desired rate and delay allowance; a Controlled-Load request uses the shared traffic fields.

sections.title: A Length-Tagged Three-Level Format
sections.content:
The appendix defines a general encoding with a message header, per-service fragments and parameters. The 32-bit message header carries the format version, currently 0, and the message length in 32-bit words, excluding the header word.

Each per-service header identifies a service, carries its break bit and gives the fragment length. Each parameter header identifies a parameter and gives its flags and data length. Lengths exclude their own header words, so a node can skip a service or parameter it does not understand. Parameter values use XDR encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message labels its service sections and parameters with their sizes. A network element can skip information it does not recognize and still find the next section.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its message formatting and usage rules raise no security issues by themselves. Using RSVP and integrated-services scheduling to provide enhanced service creates a need to control and authenticate access to that service.

The RFC points to RFC 2205, RFC 2211 and RFC 2212 for that access-control requirement. It also refers to a separate RSVP cryptographic-authentication specification for protecting message integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: The object formats do not provide access control. Networks that offer enhanced service need to check who may request it and protect RSVP messages against changes.
